articles.title: Venezuela: Regional Movement Trends and Patterns LAC - January – June 2026
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. REGIONAL PANORAMA The first half of 2026 marked a further shift away from the large-scale northbound transit movements that defined previous years. Human mobility across Latin America and the Caribbean became less concentrated along a small number of transit routes and increasingly reflected a mix of regular migration, return movements, localized cross-border mobility and movements within South America. Irregular northbound transit continued to fall across several of the region’s principal routes. Northbound movements through the Darién dropped to just 280 during the reporting period, irregular entries recorded in Honduras were 74 per cent lower than in the first half of 2025, and movement monitoring in Guatemala recorded a 62 per cent decline. These reductions point to a continued slowdown in the transit corridors that, until recently, carried large numbers of migrants and refugees towards North America. At the same time, United Sates of America (U.S.) Southwest land-border encounters increased by 26 per cent between the first and second quarters of 2026, indicating a moderate rise after historically low levels at the beginning of the year. The decline in irregular transit did not mean less mobility overall. Several countries in South America recorded increases in regular cross-border movements, including Colombia, Ecuador and Paraguay. Movement patterns also differed increasingly by nationality. Cuban mobility through Panama and Honduras declined sharply, while asylum applications and migration balances pointed to continued arrivals and settlement in countries such as Brazil and Uruguay. Haitian migration was increasingly facilitated through regular pathways, including family reunification programmes connecting Haiti and Brazil. Return movements became more visible across the region. Since early 2025 over 271,000 Mexicans were returned from the U.S. returns to Guatemala and Honduras increased by 44 per cent compared with the first half of 2025, removals from the U.S. continued to rise, and southbound movements through Panama remained a notable feature of regional mobility. Forced removals, transfer arrangements, assisted voluntary return programmes and spontaneous returns all contributed to a more complex return landscape, increasing demand for reception, reintegration and protection support in countries of return. Reasons for movement varied across countries where data were available. In Mexico, protection monitoring found that violence-related factors were the main drivers of departure, with 54% of respondents citing violence, threats, or intimidation. This was particularly common among Hondurans, 68 per cent of whom reported violence, threats, or intimidation as their main reason for leaving, and Haitians, among whom 74 per cent cited general insecurity. In contrast, Venezuelans reported a more balanced mix of protection-related (55%) and economic (43%) reasons for departure in this country6. In Guatemala, most refugees and migrants (76%) identified economic factors as their primary reason for migrating. Intended destinations differed by route, with Venezuela, Colombia, and Peru among the most frequently reported destinations in southbound movements. Across migration routes, refugees and migrants reported high levels of unmet basic needs, particularly food assistance (98% of refugees and migrants surveyed in Peru and 72% in Guatemala8), as well as water, sanitation and hygiene support. Moreover, and despite lower volumes on several major transit routes, protection concerns remained acute. At least 113 deaths were recorded across the Americas during the reporting period, with drowning, environmental exposure and hazardous transportation among the leading causes. Internal displacement also remained severe, particularly in Haiti, while evidence from Ecuador, Colombia, and Honduras highlighted the growing influence of violence, insecurity and environmental pressures on population movements within countries.

articles.title: Centuries-old cemetery helps scientists link climate shocks to Industrial Revolution disease
articles.description: During England's Industrial Revolution, when the country's farming-based economy transformed into an industrial one between roughly 1760 and 1840, pollution, harsh working conditions, inadequate housing and limited access to sunlight drove disease. Rickets, in which the growing skeleton fails to properly mineralize, was commonplace among children. Traditionally, urbanization, latitude and socioeconomic status were considered the main drivers. A factor that has largely been overlooked is climate.

articles.title: A carefully timed pair of light pulses can amplify the motion of atomic layers in a quantum material
articles.description: The principle "Work smarter, not harder!" apparently also applies to controlling quantum materials with light. Many of their fascinating properties depend on how the atoms are arranged in the crystal. Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to alter these structures in a targeted way—the light first excites electrons, whose changed energy and dynamics exert forces on the atomic nuclei and can thereby set the atoms in motion. Such processes unfold within femtoseconds, a millionth of a billionth of a second.
